I agree with @5DN1L that the problem difficulty is unsuitable for clash of code. While the solution's code is seemingly simple, it relies on quite a bit of math underneath it.

To demonstrate the complexity, here's the solution of the task that must be known to justify the example solution:

1) First we decide that we'll be counting the contribution of each bit in the initial bitstring to the final XOR separately.
2) Secondly we must observe that non-starting bits do not contribute to the result: for each subsequence containing bit [[i]] at position [[k]], we can pair it with another subsequence that contains bit [[i]] at position [[k]] by toggling whether the first bit is part of this subsequence. That means that our bit [[i]] will appear at any position [[k]] in an even number of subsequences, thus cancelling out in the final XOR. So we must only solve for the first bit.
3) For the first bit: we again decide that we'll be counting the contribution to each bit of the result separately (similar to (2)).
4) For the result bit [[k]], we must count the number of subsequences that place the first bit at position [[k]] (where [[k]]th bit represents 2^k). That means that among [[n-1]] other bits in the string we choose exactly [[k]] to include in such subsequence. That's [[n-1]] chose [[k]] different subsequences. In the resulting substring bit [[k]] will be set if and only if the number of these subsequences is odd, that is if [[binom(n-1, k) mod 2]] is [[1]].
5.1) Now one can use a builtin library to calculate the binomial coefficients for all k=0..n-1, take it mod 2, and multiply the remainder by 2^k and sum all these values up.
5.2) Alternatively, one might know about the pascal's triangle and how the next row is the previous row + previous row shifted by 1, and that you can take all entries mod 2, and come up with the following algorithm to calculate the result (which is pretty neat):

    set result = 1
    repeat n-1 times
        set result = result ^ (result << 1)
    return result

5.3) Alternatively, one might know about the Lucas's theorem, or in particular the following consequences:
    For a prime P, (N choose K) is divisble by P if and only if one of the digits of the base-p representation of N is greater than the corresponding digit of K
or in particular for the case we are intersted in, for P=2:
    N choose K is odd if and only if the binary representation of K is a submask of the binary representation of N

5.3 is the fact that is being relied upon in the example solution

Moreover, it further requires knowing the following:

5.3.1) To iterate through all submasks of a given binary mask, you can use the following loop

    set submask = mask
    loop
        <process submask>
        when submask == 0
            break
        set submask = (submask - 1) & mask


Remark: the example solutions implements an exponential power algorithm only to use it for getting powers of two, which can be done simply with (1ll << submask)

General
* While the solution isn't complex, the problem may be more difficult than it appears because discovering the underlying pattern requires understanding how subsequence length, XOR cancellation and combinatorics interact. It's probably more suitable as an Easy or Medium puzzle than a clash of code challenge.
